steps.title: Import required Node.js modules
steps.instruction: Import the required Node.js modules: 'fs' for file system operations and 'path' for path manipulation.
steps.hint: Use the require() function to import Node.js core modules. Place these imports at the top of your file.
steps.seedCode: // Import the required Node.js modules here
steps.expectedOutcome: The fs and path modules are imported and ready to use in your middleware.
successCriteria: fs and path modules are imported using require()
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the required Node.js modules. The fs module will handle file operations, and path will help with file path manipulation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've imported some modules, but make sure to import both 'fs' and 'path' using require().
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are missing or incorrect. You need to import both 'fs' and 'path' modules using require().

steps.title: Create the middleware function structure
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'requestLogger' that takes three parameters: req, res, and next. The function body can be empty for now.
steps.hint: Remember that middleware functions in Express/Node.js typically follow this signature: function(req, res, next) { ... }
steps.seedCode:
// Import the required Node.js modules here

// Create your requestLogger middleware function here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a function named requestLogger with three parameters (req, res, next) and an empty function body.
successCriteria: A function named 'requestLogger' exists with three parameters: req, res, and next
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the middleware function structure with the correct signature.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function is named 'requestLogger' and accepts three parameters: req, res, and next.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function structure doesn't match what's needed. Remember to create a function named 'requestLogger' with three parameters: req, res, and next.

steps.title: Define log file path
steps.instruction: Inside your requestLogger middleware function, create a variable named 'logFilePath' that points to 'logs/requests.log' using path.join() with __dirname.
steps.hint: Use path.join(__dirname, 'logs', 'requests.log') to create the full file path.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a file path variable
const filePath = path.join(__dirname, 'data', 'output.txt');
steps.expectedOutcome: The middleware function now contains a 'logFilePath' variable that stores the full path to the log file.
successCriteria: A 'logFilePath' variable is defined inside the requestLogger function using path.join(__dirname, 'logs', 'requests.log').
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the log file path using path.join(). This ensures the path works correctly regardless of the operating system.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using path.join() with __dirname and the correct folder structure ('logs/requests.log').
steps.feedbackWrong: The log file path wasn't defined correctly. Remember to use path.join(__dirname, 'logs', 'requests.log') inside your middleware function.

steps.title: Create logs directory if it doesn't exist
steps.instruction: Inside your requestLogger function, use fs.existsSync() to check if the logs directory exists, and create it with fs.mkdirSync() if it doesn't.
steps.hint: First check if the directory exists, then create it only if it doesn't exist. You'll need to use the path you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: The middleware function will now ensure the logs directory exists before attempting to write log files.
successCriteria: The requestLogger function contains code that checks for the logs directory existence and creates it if missing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the directory check and creation logic. This ensures the logs directory exists before we try to write files to it.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking if the directory exists and creating it only when it doesn't. Check your logic carefully.
steps.feedbackWrong: The directory check and creation logic is missing or incorrect. Remember to use fs.existsSync() to check and fs.mkdirSync() to create the directory if it doesn't exist.

steps.title: Extract request information
steps.instruction: Inside your requestLogger middleware function, extract the request method, URL, and current timestamp into variables named method, url, and timestamp.
steps.hint: Access req.method and req.url. Use Date.now() or new Date() for the timestamp.
steps.expectedOutcome: The middleware function now contains variables storing the request method, URL, and timestamp.
successCriteria: Variables named method, url, and timestamp are declared inside the requestLogger function, with method and url extracted from the req object, and timestamp set to the current time.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully extracted the request method, URL, and timestamp. These are the key pieces of information we'll log for each request.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've extracted some request information, but not all three required variables. Make sure you have variables named method, url, and timestamp inside the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The request information extraction isn't complete. Inside the requestLogger function, create variables for the request method (req.method), URL (req.url), and current timestamp.

steps.title: Format the log message
steps.instruction: Inside your requestLogger function, create a formatted log message string that includes the current timestamp, request method, and request URL.
steps.hint: Use a template literal to combine the timestamp, method, and URL into a single string with clear formatting.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: formatting a message with variables
const message = `${timestamp} - ${method} ${url}`;
steps.expectedOutcome: A formatted log message string is created inside the middleware function.
successCriteria: A log message string is created that includes timestamp, method, and URL with proper formatting.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a formatted log message that includes all the essential request information.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your log message includes the timestamp, method, and URL in a single formatted string.
steps.feedbackWrong: The log message formatting isn't quite right. You need to create a string that combines the timestamp, method, and URL values.

steps.title: Write log to file
steps.instruction: Inside your requestLogger function, use fs.appendFile() to write the formatted log message to the log file, adding a newline character at the end.
steps.hint: Call fs.appendFile() with the log file path, the log message plus '\n' for a newline, and a callback function to handle any errors.
steps.expectedOutcome: The middleware will now write each request log to the specified file with proper formatting.
successCriteria: fs.appendFile() is called with the log file path, the log message plus a newline character, and an error-handling callback.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented file writing for your request logger. The middleware will now persistently record each request.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using fs.appendFile() with the correct arguments: file path, log message with newline, and a callback function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to use fs.appendFile() to write the formatted log message to the log file. Remember to add '\n' for proper line breaks.

steps.title: Handle file write errors
steps.instruction: Add error handling to the fs.appendFile() call inside your requestLogger function. Use a callback function to check for errors and log them to the console if they occur.
steps.hint: The fs.appendFile() method accepts a callback function as its last parameter. This callback receives an error argument that you can check.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fs.appendFile() call now includes error handling that logs any file write errors to the console.
successCriteria: The fs.appendFile() callback checks for errors and logs them to console when they occur
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added error handling to the file write operation. This ensures your middleware won't fail silently if there are file system issues.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking the error parameter in the callback and logging it to the console when an error occurs.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error handling isn't quite right. Remember that fs.appendFile() takes a callback function that receives an error parameter. Check if that error exists and log it.

steps.title: Call next() to continue request chain
steps.instruction: Inside your requestLogger middleware function, call the next() function after the file write operation to pass control to the next middleware in the chain.
steps.hint: Add next() after the fs.appendFile callback to ensure the request continues processing.
steps.expectedOutcome: The middleware will properly continue the request-response cycle by passing control to the next middleware function after logging.
successCriteria: The requestLogger function calls next() after the file write operation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've correctly added next() to continue the middleware chain. This ensures requests don't get stuck in your logging middleware.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure next() is called after the file write operation, not before it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The middleware needs to call next() to pass control to the next middleware. Add next() after the fs.appendFile callback.

steps.title: Export the middleware function
steps.instruction: Export the requestLogger middleware function using module.exports so it can be imported in other files.
steps.hint: Add an export statement at the end of your file using module.exports.
steps.expectedOutcome: The requestLogger function will be exported and ready to be imported in other files.
successCriteria: The requestLogger function is exported using module.exports.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully exported the middleware function. It's now ready to be imported and used in other parts of your application.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're exporting the requestLogger function using module.exports.
steps.feedbackWrong: The export statement is missing or incorrect. Use module.exports to export the requestLogger function.
